lines.note: Gyanetsu is glossed as recurring fever without chills. The weakened n is read from its surviving strokes and the headword sequence, corroborated by the supplied NINJAL index; it is not Cuiaret.
Gibasoo is identified only as an herb of this name. The damaged a in the headword is compatible with that reading; no botanical species is supplied beyond the source.

runs.text: Hũa erua, ou fula que nace della.

lines.note: Gibooshi names an herb or the flower arising from it. Fula is retained as printed, not replaced with flor or folha merely to resemble modern Portuguese.

runs.text: Maçanetas de pao, ou latão que es-

lines.note: A separate gibooshi denotes wooden or brass finials. The circumflex matches the preceding headword, while es- begins the verb estão on the next row.

runs.text: tão por remate dos balauſtes, daſpontes, &c.

lines.note: The finials cap balusters on bridges and similar structures. The tight daſpontes and historical balauſtes are retained rather than normalized.

runs.text: Cajado de jugar a chòca ao modo de

lines.note: Gichoo is a stick for a Japanese ball game, compared with Portuguese choca. The grave in chòca and caron on the headword are separate graphic details.
Gichoo de tama wo utsu means striking a ball with the stick. The Japanese ends before Dar, which begins its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: com o cajado na choca, ou

lines.note: Completes Dar: strike with the stick or play choca. This explains the Japanese game through a familiar comparison, not an assertion that the two games have identical rules.
Gidarin is equated with chausu, a millstone for grinding tea. The scan supports the long s in Chauſu; the Portuguese Mo and chà are retained as printed.
Gidatte describes taking offence or becoming irritated. The damaged double t is supported by the repeated example below and the supplied lexical index, rather than by modernizing the word.

runs.text: em couſas que não ha pera que ſe agastar. Vt,

lines.note: The irritation concerns things that give no proper reason for anger. Preserve the printed short s in agastar despite the long-s form in the preceding line.
The example describes a person who speaks in an unnecessarily affronted manner. Guidatte and the joined monouoyǔ correct OCR Gaidatte while retaining the impression's word division.

runs.text: que ſe a gasta, ou perturba por qualquer couſa,

lines.note: The person becomes angry or disturbed over anything. The unusual printed space in a gasta is retained rather than silently removing it.
Alternatively the person takes unnecessary offence or insists on misplaced dignity. Deſneceßario retains the ligature and explains the excessive nature of the reaction.
Gihei denotes soldiers or a body of fighting men. Gui- begins the repeated headword in the example on the next row.
Gihei wo okosu or moyoosu means raising or assembling troops. The letter l introduces an alternative verb rather than belonging to the Japanese.
Completes the translation assembling troops, then gives gihei wo aguru as another equivalent. The native scan supports guerra with rr and Guifeiuo without the OCR's extra i.

runs.text: Bailo de molheres que tem por of-

lines.note: Gigaku is described here as dancing by women who perform professionally. Preserve this source-specific gloss rather than replacing it with the modern historical definition of the art form.
Completes officio: their occupation is dancing and entertaining others. The divided word belongs to the Portuguese explanation, not a Japanese entry.

runs.text: Molher que tem eſte officio de bai-

lines.note: Gijo names a woman in the profession just described. Bai- begins bailar, continued below with singing as another activity.
Completes bailar and adds singing to the performer's profession. This short row closes Guigio before the separate deliberation entry.

runs.text: Determinação, ou aſſento, que ſe faz

lines.note: Gijoo denotes a determination or decision reached about a matter. Determinação is one printed word, not OCR Deter minação.
The decision concerns some matter. Gijoo suru begins the verbal example, with l introducing its alternative past form below.
Xita completes the present/past alternatives suru and shita. The second example says that determinations or opinions vary; machimachi nari is a complete Japanese predication.
The Portuguese translates the preceding example as differing determinations or opinions. The apparently superfluous r in determinarçoens is visible and retained as a printed anomaly.
Gigi suru is described as being confuted or left convinced. Keep the joined Guiguiſuru; the following line specifies the inability to answer.
The person cannot reply. This completes the argumentative sense of ficar convencido rather than describing mere positive agreement.
A separate gigi means something grand and magnificent. The following example and ceremonial scene explain this sense, distinct from the preceding verb.

Gigi tootoni gozaru characterizes something as imposing or magnificent. The ending reads ni rather than the OCR's mi; the damaged repeated expression is retained without reconstructing a different classical formula.

runs.text: & excellente, & de fausto, como onde ha mu-

lines.note: The description adds excellence and splendour, introducing an example with many people. The physical ending is mu-, not OCR mus-; fausto retains its printed short s.

runs.text: ta gente bem ornada por ordem, &c.

lines.note: Mu- plus ta gives the printed muta, describing many well-adorned people arranged in order. No unprinted i is inserted to normalize it to muita.
Gizetsu means breaking friendship, paraphrased as naka wo chigoo. Amiza- starts the Portuguese noun amizade on the following row.
The example says Pedro and Joao are estranged. Pedroto belongs wholly to the upright Japanese sentence, not partly to the italic example marker as in the OCR styling.
Ru completes degozaru. The Portuguese says Pedro and Joao have fallen out; Ioão begins with I, not the OCR's c.
Desavindos completes the alternative description, at odds with one another. The historical u/v spelling and long s remain unchanged.
Gijuu is explained by ari and hai, ant and fly. A faint grave mark survives above the final u; the Japanese f represents the historical h-row sound rather than an error in fai.
Gimon is explained through doubting and asking. The initial G and Portuguese Duuidar are supported by the scan, replacing OCR Cuimon and Luuidar.
Gin means silver, with shirokane as its Japanese synonym. This brief metal entry is separate from the incense implement described next.

runs.text: Hũa folhaſinha como de vidro, ou

lines.note: Another gin is a small thin sheet compared with glass or crystal. Folhaſinha is the printed diminutive; the material comparison continues below.

runs.text: criſtal que poem nos perfumadores ſobre a cin-

lines.note: The sheet is placed in an incense burner over hot ash. Cin- begins cinza, not a new noun at the next line.

runs.text: za quente, & ſobre eſta folha que às vezes

lines.note: Completes cinza quente and introduces what is placed on the sheet. The relative clause notes that its material can vary.

runs.text: he de prata, ou ouro, poẽ o cheiro, aguila, &c.

lines.note: The sheet may be silver or gold and supports fragrant substances such as aguila. The source describes its use; no specific modern mineral identification is imposed on gin.
Ginnan is the fruit of the ichoo tree, as ichoo no mi explains. Preserve the spelling Guinan, with one written n at the internal boundary, rather than modernizing it.
The tree is named Ichǒ and the fruit is eaten roasted. The mark on Ichǒ is caron-shaped, not the baseline's grave; the word is embedded in the Portuguese naming clause.
The additional sense is the same tree itself. Ameſma is tightly joined in the impression and is retained as printed.
A homographic gin'an is a silver-covered saddle, literally shirokane no kura. The initial G distinguishes the printed headword from OCR Cuinan.
Prateada completes the description of the horse's saddle as silvered. It is body text, not a catchword or page signature.
Ginbaku is silver leaf, literally shirokane no haku. The synonym begins with a visible capital X, correcting the baseline's lowercase x.
The leaves are made of beaten silver. This completes folhas de and specifies how the thin material is produced.
Ginban is a silvered table or tray. Ta- begins taboleiro on the next line; the Japanese paraphrase names a silver ban.
Completes taboleiro prateado, a silvered tray or board. Preserve the Portuguese line division rather than repeating the initial ta.
Ginbyoo denotes silvered folding screens. The gloss reads Beǒbos rather than OCR Bebbos; the unusual loanword spelling and its small caron are retained from the impression.
Ginbon is a silver tray, literally shirokane no bon. The Portuguese offers a second equivalent below without a clearly printed comma before ou.
Bacio de prata completes the alternative, a silver basin or platter. Its vessel sense belongs to the tray definition.
Ginkaku is explained as a silver house or rich buildings. The Portuguese plural is retained even though the Japanese paraphrase does not mark number.
The buildings are adorned with silver. Ornadas is continuous, correcting the OCR's spurious internal space.
Ginkoo is going along reciting, as ginjite yuku explains. The Portuguese cõ- continues as consigo below and retains its printed nasal abbreviation.

The verses are repeated to oneself with enjoyment. The vowel after g is badly abraded; gosto is the chosen reading, supported by surviving ink and the parallel pleasure-and-reflection gloss below rather than OCR gesto. The aligned short s is retained.
Ginkooka denotes a very courteous person in this gloss. The caron is visible; no unprinted modern accent is added to cortes.
Ginga is equated with Amanogawa and the Milky Way. The weakened ct sequence supports Vialactea rather than OCR Vialacea; the printed compound is retained without modern spacing.
Ginji, ginzuru, ginjita gives the principal forms for reciting or intoning verses. The Portuguese com continues into sigo on the following row without an added hyphen.

runs.text: ſigo com goſto, & conſideração. ¶ Item, So-

lines.note: The recitation is to oneself with pleasure and reflection. A further sense begins with So-, completed as soar below.
The additional sense is sounding or resonating: kaze ni ginzuru. The Japanese example is upright between two italic Portuguese spans.
Ginmi is explained by savouring or tasting thoughtfully. Guinjite is partly abraded but coherent with the adjacent recitation entry; the final Portuguese word is prouar, not a line-end proua-.

runs.text: cõ gosto. ¶ Item, Com o entẽdimento, &

lines.note: The first sense is tasting with pleasure; the next transfers that activity to the understanding and will. The printed short s in gosto is retained.

runs.text: vontade conſiderar cõ goſto as couſas. Vt,

lines.note: The figurative sense is considering matters with pleasure through understanding and will. This prepares the religious example below.
The Japanese example applies ginmi to the things of God. Deusno belongs to the Japanese sentence with its attached particle, not to a Portuguese prose definition.
Completes Goſtar: savouring the things of God by meditating on them. The joined object ending in meditandoas is retained.
Ginpai means a silver drinking cup, with shirokane no sakazuki as its paraphrase. The Portuguese supplies two vessel terms across the line break.
A silver cup or goblet completes the definition. The short row belongs to Guinpai, not to the following wall entry.
Ginpeki is a silvered wall. Pratea continues into prateada on the next row without a visible terminal hyphen; the right-hand rule is present in the crop.
The example describes setting or arranging jewels on a silvered wall. The scan supports the short r of tçuranuru, consistent with tsuranuru, rather than OCR tçutanuru.

runs.text: Ornar de pedras precioſas a parede prateada.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains the example as adorning the silvered wall with precious stones. This confirms the decorative action without modernizing the Japanese verb.
Ginkyoku is harmony or pleasant singing. The initial and ending are worn but support Guinqiocu; the source's Armonia lacks a modern initial h.
Ginsan is another silver-cup term, given the same Japanese paraphrase as ginpai. Retain the printed long s in the headword.
Completes the silver drinking-vessel gloss. Its repetition is genuine and should not be removed as duplicate OCR text.
Ginsu is equated directly with shirokane, silver. The scan supports capital G and the long s; the separator after i is a comma.
Ginsei is the voice used in reciting verses. Guinzuru koe explains it in Japanese; pro- starts the Portuguese verb prova below.

runs.text: ua verſos repetindoos, ou entoandoos cõſigo.

lines.note: The voice belongs to someone trying or reciting verses, repeating or intoning them to himself. The joined pronouns in repetindoos and entoandoos are preserved.
Ginsen means silver coin, literally shirokane no zeni. The headword's tilde abbreviates the nasal ending and is not a long-vowel accent.
Ginshi is silver thread, directly equated with shirokane no ito. The following line gives its use in a richly ornamented setting.
Ginshi kinchoo wo tsunagu describes tying gold-thread curtains with silver thread. Preserve the caron and the word order rather than adding an unprinted instrumental particle.

runs.text: de prata as cortinas tecidas com fio douro.

lines.note: The curtains are woven with gold thread and tied with silver thread. Douro retains the source's contracted spelling.
Ginshin is a silver needle, explained as shirokane no hari. The initial is G rather than OCR C; pra- begins prata below.
Ginshin wo hineru means twisting the silver needle. The Portuguese explains an insertion and divides agulha after its initial a-.
The silver needle is inserted into flesh while being twisted. Preserve the joined deprata and torcendoa; this completes the historical account of the needle's use.
Ginshoo denotes the wind sounding in pine trees. Matsu ni ginzuru supplies the Japanese paraphrase, while the Portuguese sentence continues below.
The sound is in the pines, completing the wind description. S. marks written usage.
Ginshoku is a silver candlestick, literally a silver toodai. The circumflex and the source's spelling Castiçal are retained.
Silver completes the candlestick definition. The line is a genuine short continuation between two full entries.
Gin'ei is composing or reciting verses, referred to ginji. Ver continues below without a visible terminal hyphen; the crop includes the rule beyond it.
Completes versos and describes intoning them to oneself. Shiika wo gin'ei su begins the example, with guin- divided at the physical edge.
Yei ſu completes gin'ei su, to recite or compose verse. The written-register label is separate from the Japanese verb.

Ginzan is a mountain of silver, literally shirokane no yama. Pra continues on the next page as ta; the separate bottom catchword anticipates that syllable and must not be absorbed into this body line.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The catchword anticipates ta. at the opening of f239, completing pra / ta across the page turn; it is not an additional body row.
